extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of 19th‑century American history and abolitionism; general readers of biographical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a biographical/historical essay about John Brown and William Lloyd Garrison, describing character, motives, rhetoric, and movement dynamics in the antebellum abolitionist movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle as standard of classification
rubrics_metrics.description: "Principle is the word I brought away with me as most familiar in their vocabulary. That is their standard of classification."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The family and associates judge people primarily by adherence to principle rather than by bravery, fame, or worldly honor. Use 'principle' as the chief lens for assessing motives and worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to Providence / higher motive vs. fame
rubrics_metrics.description: They appealed not to the world's opinion but to the Eternal God; they 'worked for a higher price than fame.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions by whether they are motivated by religious/ethical conviction or by desire for worldly applause; praise is given where motive is devotion to a higher end rather than pursuit of fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of vindictive spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: "Utter absence of the slightest vindictive spirit, even in words."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non‑vindictiveness (even in speech) is presented as a moral virtue and a criterion for favorable judgment of individuals and families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal virtues: rectitude, kindness, foresight, activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The father is described as a person of 'absolute rectitude, thoughtful kindness, unfailing foresight, and inexhaustible activity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character assessment prioritizes honesty/rectitude, thoughtfulness/kindness, foresight (planning/management), and industriousness as markers of moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to sacrifice / economic self‑denial for a cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Family members accept privation so men may 'continue their Kansas work'; 'I sometimes think that is what we came into the world for — to make sacrifices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sacrifice and material self‑denial for the sake of a larger cause are framed positively and weigh in favorable evaluations of commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious conviction tied to radicalism
rubrics_metrics.description: John Brown 'is almost the only radical abolitionist I have ever known who was not more or less radical in religious matters also. His theology was Puritan, like his practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious seriousness and doctrinal rigor are considered integral to (and explanatory of) radical abolitionist commitment; evaluate ideological stances in light of underlying theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicalism: subordinating words to action
rubrics_metrics.description: He had 'an almost exaggerated aversion to words and speeches, and a profound conviction of the importance of bringing all questions to a direct issue, and subjecting every theory to the test of practical application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor practical, action‑oriented approaches that test theory by application rather than rhetorical debate; practical effectiveness is a key evaluative dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/presentational traits as leadership markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Garrison identified by 'firm and well-built person, his sonorous voice, and the grave and iron strength of his face' — 'the visible embodiment of something deeper... moral strength and force.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical presence, commanding voice, and an appearance conveying moral force are treated as legitimate indicators of leadership and centrality at conventions or public gatherings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical style: commanding tone, reiteration, scriptural invective
rubrics_metrics.description: His utterance was 'grave, powerful, with little variety...monotonous, sometimes fatiguing, but always controlling.' He 'constantly reiterated and intrenched his argument with ample details' and used 'mainly scriptural' invective and newspaper cuttings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess rhetorical effectiveness by control and persistence (repetition, use of authority like scripture), even if stylistically severe; use of documentary evidence (newspaper cuttings) is noted as a persuasive technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone moderation vs. excessive harshness
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of Garrison included 'excessive harshness of language' and contemporaries noted they 'do not pretend to like or to approve the tone of Garrison's pointed censures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate public rhetoric for tone: excessive harshness or invective is a common internal and external criticism and weakens appeal to some audiences, even if rhetorically powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility vs. arrogance in leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Charge from associates that Garrison manifested 'arrogance' — 'You exalt yourself too much' — and criticisms that he wanted others to 'live out William Lloyd Garrison, not the convictions of our own souls.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal humility and allowance for conscience in followers are criteria for good leadership; perceived self‑exaltation or enforcing conformity is a serious internal critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movement unity and internal divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: There 'raged within the anti‑slavery ranks...a hostility' that 'vastly embarrassed the whole enterprise' and led to rival camps (Old vs New Organization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess movement effectiveness by internal cohesion; factionalism and schisms are presented as important negative factors that can impede reform success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral absolutism vs. recognition of human complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The author critiques the abolitionist tendency to treat 'the least of sins [as] infinite' and to pronounce slaveholders 'without excuse', noting that 'men are...very often, better than the laws under which they live.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance moral condemnation with recognition of context (ignorance, heredity, environment); uncompromising absolutism is powerful but can be based on an 'untruth' and thus also a weakness.
